problem: Video-based LVLM navigators must keep long visual history for trajectory consistency and act with low latency. Fixed-frame sampling loses temporal density, token merging/pooling destroys the 2D spatial grid (conflicting with M-RoPE/DeepStack), and autoregressive action decoding is slow.
motivation: Real-time control in continuous environments needs both long-horizon memory and fast decisions. An attention analysis shows the most recent frames get most of the attention (the last 4 of 12 frames get over 50%), so uniform-resolution history wastes tokens. Latency also grows almost linearly with the number of output tokens.
key_idea: Mimic human episodic memory with a pyramidal-resolution history (recent frames high-res, old frames downsampled in pixel space) and procedural memory with single-token mid-level action vocabulary so an action is decoded in one forward pass.
insight: Pixel-space downsampling keeps the uniform 2D token grid and gives a longer look-back at a fixed token budget. Ablation: the ascending pyramid (high-res recent) is best, while descending is far worse (R2R SR 43.8 vs 53.8). Single-token actions give a 7x speedup (2 to 14 FPS) and also improve accuracy (R2R SR +1.8, RxR SR +2.1) over textual mid-level actions. DAgger data gives the largest data gains.
method: Episodic memory (pyramidal resolution): frames are split into immediate/short-term/long-term tiers by boundaries B_short and B_long and rescaled to 512/256/128 px before tokenization, keeping the token budget constant (long-term tokens no more than one immediate frame).
Pixel-space compression vs token merging: downsampling before the visual encoder preserves the uniform spatial grid, so it is compatible with M-RoPE and DeepStack.
Pyramid variants: U-shaped, descending and ascending resolution profiles were explored; ascending (recent = high-res) is used, with a best config of 4 immediate / 8 short / 32 long frames.

Procedural memory (fast action): 10 existing single vocabulary tokens are repurposed as atomic mid-level actions (stop; forward 25/50/75 cm; turn left/right 15/30/45°), so the action comes from one forward pass.
Architecture: Qwen3-VL (4B/8B) with a visual encoder over selected frames plus the instruction; monocular RGB only.
Training: SFT with cross-entropy on the augmented action token, 1 epoch, batch size 128, LR 1e-5 cosine, on R2R, RxR, EnvDrop, 416K ScaleVLN, 557K human trajectories and 278K DAgger samples.

setting.training_data: R2R + RxR train, EnvDrop augmentation, 416K ScaleVLN pairs (HM3D/Gibson), 557K human navigation trajectories (NaVILA), 278K DAgger synthetic samples
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB video (single view, 90° HFOV), no depth/odometry/panorama
setting.action_space: low-level discrete actions via 10 single-token mid-level actions (forward 25/50/75 cm, turn 15/30/45°, stop)

numbers.extra: full training corpus incl. ScaleVLN, human, DAgger, EnvDrop data
trained exclusively on R2R train split
numbers.evidence: Table (Cross-dataset performance on RxR-CE Val Unseen)

numbers_note: Table 1 prints RxR OS only in ablation tables; the RxR main-table columns are NE/SR/SPL.
results: MemVLN-8B reaches 58.4 SR on R2R-CE and MemVLN-4B reaches 66.5 SR / 57.4 SPL on RxR-CE with monocular RGB only, beating StreamVLN-7B (56.9 SR R2R; 52.9 SR RxR). Fast action gives 14 FPS (7x faster than autoregressive decoding), and R2R-only zero-shot transfer to RxR beats NaVILA (38.4 vs 34.3 SR).
limitations: Relies on GPU acceleration and was not scaled to very large models; edge deployment is untested.
Evaluated only in simulation (Habitat R2R-CE/RxR-CE), no real-robot experiments.
Adding human and ScaleVLN data slightly hurt performance in the ablation, and SPL on R2R does not beat StreamVLN-7B.
